title: 1950 Australian National Airways Douglas DC-4 crash
summary: The Amana departed Perth for Adelaide but crashed 22 minutes after takeoff while flying at unusually low altitude. Witnesses observed rough engine running and backfiring; engines periodically lost power completely. Investigation found significant corrosion product and water in the fuel system of at least two engines, which caused rough running and temporary loss of power from all engines.
probable_cause: Water in the fuel system caused corrosion and loss of power from all engines on at least one occasion during the climb.

factors.evidence: a significant amount of corrosion product was found in the fuel system within two of the engines
temporary loss of power from all engines on at least one occasion
aircraft was flying at a lower altitude than usual for the daily Skymaster services
crashed 22 minutes after take-off, 35 mi east of Perth Airport
All 29 occupants were killed in the accident either from multiple injuries and burns, or from incineration

events.text: Amana departed Perth Airport at 9:55 pm for Adelaide
Radio report received from Amana at 10:00 pm advising it was on course and climbing to 9,000 feet
Aircraft heard flying low over York area with changing engine noise; all engine noise ceased briefly then returned as very loud high-pitched scream
Bright flash of white light observed 28 nmi east of Perth Airport, followed by loud crashing noise and yellow glow of fire
Trans Australia Airlines aircraft passed over band of fire on ground; Amana had failed to report position at Cunderdin

title: TWA 903
summary: Flight 903 departed Cairo at 23:35 with 48 passengers and 7 crew for Rome in good weather. As the aircraft was climbing at 10,000 feet, the crew reported that the number three engine was on fire and requested priority return to Cairo. As the aircraft was returning to Cairo, the number three engine separated from the aircraft. The crew attempted a forced landing in the desert about 65 miles north-northwest of Cairo, killing all 55 occupants. Investigation determined the cause was failure of the rear master rod bearing on the number three engine due to sludge buildup in the crankpins blocking oil flow.
probable_cause: Failure of the rear master rod bearing on the number three engine. The failure caused the rear crankpin to overheat and fail, whereupon all the rear connecting rods failed, tearing through cylinder walls and crankcase. Sludge buildup in the crankpins blocking oil flow was thought to be the root cause.

factors.evidence: the crew reported that its number three engine was on fire
Sludge buildup in the crankpins, blocking oil flow was thought to be the root cause
the number three engine was on fire

events.text: Aircraft departed Cairo at 23:35 with 48 passengers and 7 crew in good weather
As aircraft climbed at 10,000 feet, number three engine caught fire
Crew reported engine fire and requested priority return to Cairo
Number three engine separated from aircraft during return; crew attempted forced landing in desert about 65 miles NNW of Cairo, all 55 occupants killed

notes: Root cause clearly identified through investigation; resulted in improved oil screens and revised oil change intervals

title: 1950 Tête de l'Obiou C-54 crash
summary: A Douglas C-54B-1-DC en route from Rome to Paris crashed into the Grande Tête de l'Obiou mountain, killing all 58 occupants. The aircraft was 40 nautical miles east of its reported position at Istres, indicating navigation error. Night was falling and the mountain was enveloped by cloud at the time of impact.

factors.evidence: Whereas the crew reported its position at Istres at 16:26, the aircraft was already some 40 nautical miles to the east
A second position report, at 16:44, put it over Montelimar, whereas it was in reality in the vicinity of the airport at Gap-Tallard
Night was falling and the mountain was enveloped by cloud at the time of the accident
the mountain was enveloped by cloud at the time of the accident
the aircraft struck the top of the 9,150-feet high Tête de l'Obiou mountain

events.text: After departing Rome Ciampino at 14:16, it crossed the Mediterranean via Bastia in Corsica
Crew reported position at Istres at 16:26 but the aircraft was already some 40 nautical miles to the east
Second position report, at 16:44, put it over Montelimar, whereas it was in reality in the vicinity of the airport at Gap-Tallard
Some fifteen minutes later, the aircraft struck the top of the 9,150-feet high Tête de l'Obiou mountain, less than six feet from the summit with all occupants killed instantly

notes: Probable cause not stated in text; navigation error and position reporting failures are documented
